extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American politics (and interested general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for communicating during national nominating conventions and the subsequent presidential campaign — including candidate acceptance letters, platforms, use of the press/telegraph, convention conduct, and managerial tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate's acceptance letter
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is for each nominated candidate to accept his nomination in a letter, sometimes as long as a pamphlet, setting forth his views of the condition of the nation and the policy which the times require; such a letter is meant to strike the keynote for the whole orchestra of orators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose an acceptance that clearly states the candidate's assessment of national condition and proposed policy; aim for a memorable 'keynote' that can be widely published, cited, praised by friends and dissected by opponents; length may be substantial (pamphlet-sized) when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform as official declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Together with the 'platform' adopted at the national party convention, [the acceptance letter] is the official declaration of party principles, to be referred to as putting the party case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the campaign's communications align with the platform; treat the platform + acceptance as the authoritative statement of party policy to which spokesmen and press should refer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and rapid dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Every incident, speech, vote, is instantly telegraphed to all the cities; frequent editions are supplemented by boards displaying the latest bulletins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rapid communications (telegraph/telephone/press bulletins) and frequent updates to ensure events are broadcast immediately; maintain central channels that send continuous bulletins and updates to press and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central organization and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: In American elections everything is held to depend on organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and maintain a central campaign organization to coordinate speaking, writing, telegraphing, and ground operations across the months-long canvass; logistical and managerial control is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle to generate enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: After a nomination: gigantic portrait hoisted, stuffed eagle carried, salvos of artillery fired, processions with bands parade the streets, ratification meetings announced, campaign clubs organized on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage visible public celebrations and symbols (portraits, parades, bands, local clubs) immediately upon success to amplify enthusiasm and create news for the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention etiquette: aspirants should not appear
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against etiquette for the aspirants themselves to appear upon the scene ... the notion that a man must not ask the people to choose him, but accept the proffered honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should generally avoid personal presence at the convention; manage appearances and communications through managers and private wires to preserve decorum and strategic distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman leadership and strict observance of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything is done according to strict rule, with a scrupulous observance of small formalities ... Of course it depends on the chairman whether or no the convention sinks into a mob. A chairman with a weak voice, or a want of prompt decision, or a suspicion of partisanship, may bring the assembly to the verge of disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a strong, decisive chair to enforce order and procedural formalities; following fine points of order and small formalities prevents chaos and disputed outcomes — important both for the convention's legitimacy and for how press covers events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers' tactical manipulation of ballots and delegates
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers hold perpetual session, reckon up their numbers, start rumours, organize raids upon less experienced delegates, 'plough around' among delegations, send 'missionaries', accredit embassies to arrange combinations, hold back votes, or throw away votes on harmless antagonists to create an impression of growing strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted outreach to wavering delegations, strategic holding or transfer of votes, planted rumours, and emissaries to form combinations; deliberate tactical maneuvers during ballot intervals can change perceptions and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balloting strategy and the importance of the 'break'
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ballot seldom decides much; repeated ballotings reveal dispositions; one balloting follows another till what is called 'the break' comes, when weaker factions transfer votes to the aspirant whose strength they see growing and the battle is decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate multiple ballots, monitor shifting loyalties, and position to be the beneficiary of the anticipated 'break' by cultivating small delegations and timing vote transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stampede/bandwagon tactics to create momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: To stampede a convention is the steadily contemplated aim of every manager who knows he cannot win on the first ballot ... he values it because it evokes an enthusiasm whose echo reverberates all over the Union ... sometimes due to the action of the aspirant himself (telegraphing transfers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or exploit moments of sudden momentum (coordinated vote transfers, public signals) so that delegations and the public jump on the bandwagon; be prepared to resist or force adjournments when advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press and rumours to shape perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists are published in the newspapers of the strength of each aspirant ... managers start rumours meant to exaggerate their resources and dishearten their opponents; the press makes the dispositions of delegates known to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately shape media narratives (publish strength lists, seed rumours, provide reporters with talking points) to influence delegates' and public perceptions; media management is integral to convention tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominating speeches: rhetorical expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator is expected to 'soar into the blue empyrean' at once. The rhetoric is usually pompous and impassioned ... To read a speech, even a short speech, from copious notes, is neither irregular nor rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft nominating speeches to be lofty and emotionally stirring to draw audible support from the crowd; reading from notes is acceptable if it achieves the desired audience reaction.
